title: Squash, merge commit, or fast-forward: pick your history shape
summary: The same branch, integrated three different ways. See exactly what each one does to history, and why --squash breaks the 'is it merged' question.
mental_model: Merge commit keeps the branch's commits and records the join. Fast-forward keeps the commits and records nothing. Squash keeps neither — it makes one new commit with the same content and no link to the branch at all.

steps.title: Look at the branch you are about to integrate
steps.why: Three commits, two of which say nothing useful. How you integrate this decides what a reader sees in six months.

steps.title: Fast-forward: keep every commit, record nothing
steps.why: main has not moved, so git slides the pointer. All three commits — 'wip dosing' included — land verbatim on main, and nothing marks them as having been a branch.
steps.expect: A straight line of four commits, no merge commit.

steps.title: Merge commit: keep every commit and the join
steps.why: `--no-ff` forces a merge commit even when a fast-forward is possible. The three commits are preserved AND the branch structure is visible forever — which `--first-parent` can then collapse when reading.
steps.expect: Full graph shows five commits; first-parent shows two.

verify.label: main's tip is a merge commit

steps.title: Squash: one new commit, no link at all
steps.why: `--squash` stages the combined result and stops. Nothing is committed and no merge is recorded — you write the commit yourself, and it has exactly one parent.
steps.expect: Changes staged, no commit yet, and no MERGE_HEAD.

steps.title: Write the commit the squash left to you
steps.why: This is the moment squash earns its keep: three throwaway messages become one message that explains the change. The content is identical to the merge; the history is not.
commands: git commit -m "Add dosing with validation and calibrated rate"

verify.label: the whole branch became one commit
…with a single parent — no merge was recorded

steps.title: The cost of squashing
steps.why: `branch --merged` does not list feature/dosing for the squash branch, because no commit of it is reachable. Git will happily offer to merge it again, and deleting it looks like losing work.
steps.expect: main lists feature/dosing as merged. squash-demo does not, despite having identical content.

verify.label: the real merge is detectable as merged

steps.title: Set a policy rather than deciding each time
steps.why: `merge.ff false` makes every merge create a merge commit; `--ff-only` on pull refuses to create accidental merges. Teams that pick one and configure it argue about history far less.

verify.label: main integrated the branch with a real merge commit
squash-demo collapsed the branch into one commit
ff-demo took all three commits with no merge commit
only the true merge makes the branch show as merged
a merge policy is set for this repository

pitfalls: After a squash merge, deleting the source branch needs `-D` — git genuinely believes the work is unmerged, and it is right about reachability.
Squash-merging a long-lived branch and then merging it again later re-applies everything and conflicts badly. Squash only short-lived branches.
`--squash` does not commit. People run it, see a clean-looking status, switch branches and lose the staged result.
GitHub's 'Squash and merge' button does exactly this, which is why the branch shows unmerged afterwards and the sha in the PR differs from the sha on main.
cheatsheet: refuse to create a merge commit
stage the result as one change, do not commit
read a merge-heavy history as a straight line
what is genuinely reachable — squashes do not count
